title: Sensory Neurons by Their Genes: the Atlas Era

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Codex accuracy gate and fixes

cards.front: In the sensory-neuron atlas lesson, a cluster is a group of cells with similar measured RNA profiles, while a {{c1::state}} is a condition an existing cell can enter and leave.
cards.quote: a state is a condition an existing cell can enter and leave

cards.front: In sensory-neuron atlases, what must a transcriptomic cluster do before it earns a functional type claim?
cards.back: It must recur across data sets and be anchored by an independent measurement. Until then it is a candidate type supporting a narrower, molecular claim.
cards.why: Its count and boundaries stay conditional on resolution, preparation and state.
cards.quote: it earns a functional type claim when it recurs and an independent measurement anchors it

cards.front: In the sensory-neuron atlas rule, what can serve as the independent anchor for a candidate cluster?
cards.back: An ending, physiology, a target, or behaviour after manipulation.
cards.quote: An independent anchor can be an ending, physiology, target or behaviour after manipulation.

cards.front: The dorsal root ganglion (DRG) holds cell bodies of neurons innervating {{c1::skin, muscle and viscera}}.
cards.quote: holds cell bodies of neurons innervating skin, muscle and viscera
cards.section: What each atlas actually counted

cards.front: Usoskin and colleagues (2015) grouped mouse lumbar DRG transcriptomes into eleven classes. What does the number eleven describe?
cards.back: The resolution one early mouse data set reached with one unsupervised clustering method, not a fixed number of DRG cell types.
cards.quote: let an unsupervised method group the single-neuron transcriptomes into eleven classes
cards.section: What each atlas actually counted

cards.front: How did Zeisel and colleagues (2018) reach seventeen mouse peripheral sensory neuron types?
cards.back: Their hierarchical taxonomy resolved eight peptidergic, six non-peptidergic and three neurofilament types.
cards.quote: resolved eight peptidergic, six non-peptidergic and three neurofilament types: seventeen
cards.section: What each atlas actually counted

cards.front: What did the 2024 cross-species integration by Bhuiyan, Renthal and colleagues contain, and from how many data sets?
cards.back: Eighteen DRG and fourteen trigeminal neuronal subtypes, from 31 DRG and trigeminal data sets across human, mouse, rat, guinea pig and two macaque species.
cards.quote: Their reference contained eighteen DRG and fourteen trigeminal neuronal subtypes.
cards.section: What each atlas actually counted

cards.front: Why do DRG atlas studies report different numbers of subtypes (eleven, seventeen, eighteen)?
cards.back: The count depends on the data set: preparation, sequencing depth and analysis all affect what is resolved.
cards.quote: preparation, sequencing depth and analysis affect what is resolved
cards.section: What each atlas actually counted

cards.front: More cells or a finer clustering setting versus a different tissue preparation: do these change an atlas in the same way?
cards.back: No. More cells, deeper sequencing or finer clustering can split a branch, which is a change of zoom. A preparation can hide RNA or whole cells, which changes what is there to see.
cards.quote: whereas a preparation can hide RNA or cells rather than merely changing the zoom
cards.section: What each atlas actually counted

cards.front: NP3, a non-peptidergic class in the 2015 mouse atlas, was linked by the authors to itch. What did that linkage rest on?
cards.back: An expression pattern only. It suggested a function but did not prove one; later itch work supplies the evidence.
cards.quote: That expression pattern suggested a function; it did not prove one
cards.section: What each atlas actually counted

cards.front: The 2024 DRG reference includes a group defined by injury-induced transcription factors, the Atf3 group. What does its presence warn a reader about?
cards.back: That an atlas can contain a state alongside types, so not every cluster in a reference is a cell type.
cards.quote: It warns that an atlas can contain a state alongside types.
cards.section: What each atlas actually counted

cards.front: In mouse DRG, do the fibre labels C, Aδ and Aβ tell you whether a neuron is a nociceptor?
cards.back: No. They name axon myelination: unmyelinated, lightly myelinated and heavily myelinated. Adult mouse tyrosine-hydroxylase-positive neurons are C-fibre low-threshold mechanoreceptors.
cards.quote: C does not mean nociceptor: adult mouse tyrosine-hydroxylase-positive neurons were identified as C-fibre LTMRs
cards.section: What each atlas actually counted

cards.front: A marker-defined mouse DRG subtype is characterized in hairy skin, and a group assumes the same response properties where that subtype innervates muscle. Which caution from the 2024 atlas applies?
cards.back: That one molecular subtype can behave differently at different innervation targets, so a subtype's physiology measured at one target does not transfer to another without testing.
cards.why: Rests on the stated caution plus the rule that a type claim needs an independent anchor in the system being claimed.
cards.quote: one molecular subtype can behave differently at different innervation targets
cards.section: What each atlas actually counted

cards.front: A Cre driver expresses Cre recombinase under a marker gene's regulatory sequences, and {{c1::CreER}} adds a tamoxifen-controlled time window.
cards.quote: A Cre driver expresses Cre recombinase under a marker gene's regulatory sequences
cards.section: From a candidate cluster to a functional test

cards.front: What does an intersectional Cre/Flp strategy restrict the label to?
cards.back: Cells that expressed both markers, since the label requires both Cre and Flp.
cards.quote: restricting the label to cells that expressed both markers
cards.section: From a candidate cluster to a functional test

cards.front: For a driver line, specificity = {{c1::labelled and marker-positive cells / all labelled cells}}.
cards.quote: specificity = labelled and marker-positive cells / all labelled cells
cards.section: From a candidate cluster to a functional test

cards.front: For a driver line, efficiency = {{c1::labelled and marker-positive cells / all marker-positive cells}}.
cards.quote: efficiency = labelled and marker-positive cells / all marker-positive cells
cards.section: From a candidate cluster to a functional test

cards.front: A CreER line labels 150 DRG neurons in a set of sections. Of those, 120 express the target marker by in situ hybridization, and the same sections hold 240 marker-positive neurons in all. Give its specificity and efficiency.
cards.back: Specificity = 120 / 150 = 80%. Efficiency = 120 / 240 = 50%. The line is mostly on target but labels only half the target population.
cards.quote: Every line has two separate quality numbers
cards.section: From a candidate cluster to a functional test

cards.front: A made-up driver line labels 400 mouse DRG neurons; 360 of them are marker-positive, and the sections contain 900 marker-positive neurons altogether. Compute specificity and efficiency, and say which number directly measures whether labelled cells are on target.
cards.back: Specificity = 360 / 400 = 90%; efficiency = 360 / 900 = 40%. Specificity directly measures whether labelled cells are on target.
cards.quote: The line can isolate the right cells for imaging
cards.section: From a candidate cluster to a functional test

cards.front: A driver line is 90% specific but only 60% efficient. The team ablates the labelled neurons and sees no behavioural deficit. What may they conclude, and why?
cards.back: Very little. A negative ablation result is weak here: killing 60% of the population and seeing no deficit does not show the population is unneeded, because 40% was never targeted.
cards.quote: killing 60% and seeing no deficit does not show the population is unneeded
cards.section: From a candidate cluster to a functional test

cards.front: With TrkC-CreER and a Ret reporter, Bai and colleagues (2015) gave 3 mg tamoxifen at E12.5 and labelled Merkel-associated Aβ SA1 endings; 0.1 mg at P5 favoured Aβ field-LTMR circumferential endings. What does the comparison support, and what does it not?
cards.back: It shows that induction conditions change which expression history is captured. It does not isolate an effect of age, because age and dose changed together.
cards.quote: Age and dose changed together, so the experiment does not isolate an effect of age.
cards.section: From a candidate cluster to a functional test

cards.front: Why is a CreER labelling difference between two induction times not evidence that SA1 neurons turn into field-LTMRs?
cards.back: The experiment never tracked the same neurons changing class; it compared two separately induced labels.
cards.quote: Nor did it track the same neurons changing class
cards.section: From a candidate cluster to a functional test

cards.front: Qi, Iskols, Sharma, Ginty and colleagues (2024) imaged calcium in genetically defined mouse DRG subtypes while indenting skin from 1 to 75 mN, heating it or cooling it. What did they report?
cards.back: Each genetically defined subtype had its own threshold and response range within the stimuli tested, and together the subtypes tiled those ranges, recruiting more subtypes as the stimulus grew stronger.
cards.quote: each genetically defined subtype had its own threshold and response range within the mechanical or thermal stimuli tested
cards.section: From a candidate cluster to a functional test

cards.front: A cluster is defined only by RNA. A driver line for its marker is built and the labelled mouse neurons respond over their own force range, unlike a neighbouring subtype. What does that add?
cards.back: An independent physiological anchor. The cluster is then more than a result of clustering settings, so its claim to be a functional type is stronger.
cards.quote: The independent physiology therefore strengthened the candidate clusters' claim to be functional types
cards.section: From a candidate cluster to a functional test

cards.front: A mouse DRG neuron fires a short high-frequency burst during in vivo GCaMP6 imaging. Can the experimenter read the exact spike count off the transient?
cards.back: No. Nearby spikes summate into one slow transient, so a single transient does not give an exact spike count, and amplitude tracks firing rate only roughly.
cards.quote: nearby spikes summate, so one transient does not give an exact spike count
cards.section: From a candidate cluster to a functional test

cards.front: What does Patch-seq do in a single cell?
cards.back: It records the neuron with a patch electrode, then aspirates and sequences that same cell, so physiology and transcriptome come from one neuron.
cards.quote: record a neuron with a patch electrode, then aspirate and sequence that same cell
cards.section: From a candidate cluster to a functional test

cards.front: A group wants to tie a precise mouse DRG firing pattern to a transcriptomic subtype. Reasoning from the lesson's limits on calcium imaging, which approach fits better, and why?
cards.back: Patch-seq. The calcium indicator's slow rise and decay blur spike counts, while patch recording plus sequencing of the same cell gives firing detail and transcriptome in one neuron.
cards.why: It rests on the stated indicator limits and on Patch-seq as the more direct bridge.
cards.quote: Patch-seq makes the bridge more direct
cards.section: From a candidate cluster to a functional test

cards.front: Sharma, Ginty and colleagues (2020) called early mouse DRG neurons unspecialized. In what sense, given that the cells were already post-mitotic sensory neurons?
cards.back: Only in subtype identity: they coexpressed transcription factors that later became restricted to particular subtype combinations over weeks.
cards.quote: they coexpressed transcription factors that later became restricted to particular subtype combinations over weeks
cards.section: The causal tests behind changing identity

cards.front: Why would deleting Ngf alone fail as a test of whether NGF shapes mouse DRG subtype identity?
cards.back: NGF keeps TrkA-expressing neurons alive, so the knockout removes cells. Altered identity could not be separated from selective survival.
cards.quote: making altered identity impossible to separate from selective survival
cards.section: The causal tests behind changing identity

cards.front: Ngf-null;Bax-null mice are profiled at P0. Which littermate control matches them, wild type or Bax-null, and why?
cards.back: Bax-null. Bax is needed for these neurons to die by apoptosis, so deleting it in both groups keeps neurons available and makes the comparison about NGF-dependent identity rather than cell loss.
cards.quote: Bax is needed for these neurons to die by apoptosis
cards.section: The causal tests behind changing identity

cards.front: What did Ngf-null;Bax-null mouse DRGs show at P0, and what claim does that support?
cards.back: Fewer transcriptionally distinct populations. NGF contributes to subtype specialization; the experiment does not show that NGF alone sets every fate.
cards.quote: At P0, the double mutants had fewer transcriptionally distinct populations.
cards.section: The causal tests behind changing identity

cards.front: Renthal and colleagues (2020) cut or crushed peripheral nerves in adult mice and sequenced single DRG nuclei. What happened to subtype identity?
cards.back: Injury suppressed subtype-marker expression, Atf3 was required for the full injury reprogramming, and identity re-emerged over a time course associated with axons regrowing to their targets.
cards.quote: Injury suppressed subtype-marker expression, and Atf3 was required for the full injury reprogramming.
cards.section: The causal tests behind changing identity

cards.front: Subtype identity returns on the same time course as regeneration. Why does the lesson say only associated with?
cards.back: Timing alone does not show that reinnervation restores identity. Apparent recovery could instead reflect which neurons survived or which were sampled.
cards.quote: Timing alone does not show that reinnervation restores identity
cards.section: The causal tests behind changing identity

cards.front: Which control argued that recovery of DRG subtype identity after nerve injury was not simply selective death of injured neurons?
cards.back: Tracing with an Atf3 injury reporter: the labelled share was unchanged from one week to two months.
cards.quote: the share labelled by an Atf3 injury reporter was unchanged from one week to two months, arguing against selective death
cards.section: The causal tests behind changing identity

cards.front: An Atf3-rich cluster appears in an injured adult mouse DRG and shrinks as axons regenerate. Type or state, and why does the answer matter?
cards.back: A state: a condition existing neurons enter and leave, not a new permanent type. The distinction matters in chronic pain, where a ganglion can be injured, inflamed or diseased.
cards.quote: An Atf3-rich cluster is a condition existing neurons enter and leave, not a new permanent type
cards.section: The causal tests behind changing identity

cards.front: A cluster appears in human DRG samples taken from inflamed ganglia but not in healthy donor tissue. Design a comparison that helps distinguish type from state.
cards.back: Sample matched healthy and inflamed ganglia with one preparation and pipeline, and trace the cells over time or across severities: a group that appears with inflammation and disappears as it resolves is a state, while one present in both is a candidate type.
cards.why: Uses the rule that a ganglion can contain states and that counts depend on preparation and state.
cards.quote: An injured, inflamed or diseased ganglion can therefore contain states.
cards.section: The causal tests behind changing identity

cards.front: Why do human DRG atlases often sequence nuclei or use tissue sections rather than dissociated whole cells?
cards.back: Donor tissue is often frozen, and large human neurons are hard to dissociate intact.
cards.quote: donor tissue is often frozen and large human neurons are hard to dissociate intact
cards.section: Human atlases: methods, markers and denominators

cards.front: MRGPRX1 localized selectively to the human class H10. Why can a mouse Mrgpr population not simply be renamed with that human gene?
cards.back: Primate MRGPRX genes have no one-to-one mouse counterparts, so the gene name does not carry a matched population across the two species.
cards.quote: Primate MRGPRX genes have no one-to-one mouse counterparts
cards.section: Human atlases: methods, markers and denominators

cards.front: Tavares-Ferreira and colleagues (2022) selected 4,356 Visium spots overlapping single neurons on human lumbar DRG sections and retained 3,952 after filtering. What fraction was retained?
cards.section: Human atlases: methods, markers and denominators

cards.front: Of twelve curated neuronal clusters in that human DRG spatial study, five were called C nociceptors. A student reports 41.67% of human DRG neurons are C nociceptors. What did the denominator count?
cards.back: Category labels, not neurons. Five of twelve is 41.67% of cluster labels, and clusters need not be equally large.
cards.why: Per-cluster spot counts come closer to abundance, because each kept spot was selected to overlap one neuron.
cards.quote: It counted category labels, not neurons.
cards.section: Human atlases: methods, markers and denominators

cards.front: In a made-up human DRG spatial study, 5,000 spots overlapping neurons were selected and 4,500 passed filtering; 1,200 retained spots fell in nociceptor-annotated clusters. State the best-supported percentage and what it is a percentage of.
cards.back: 1,200 / 4,500 = 26.7% of kept spots fall in nociceptor clusters. It describes spots in the sampled sections, not the proportion of human DRG neurons.
cards.quote: They still describe sampled sections, not all human DRG neurons.
cards.section: Human atlases: methods, markers and denominators

cards.front: TAC1 and CALCA, encoding substance P and CGRP, were broadly expressed across human nociceptor clusters. What did the authors suggest follows?
cards.back: That the mouse peptidergic / non-peptidergic split may not transfer to human DRG as a clean binary.
cards.quote: the mouse peptidergic/non-peptidergic split may not transfer as a clean binary
cards.section: Human atlases: methods, markers and denominators

cards.front: One workflow across mouse, guinea pig, macaque and human DRG put Tafa4 mainly in mouse C-LTMRs but human TAFA4 strongest in NTRK2- and SCN5A-positive Aδ-LTMRs, confirmed by in situ hybridization. What should a group planning a human study conclude first?
cards.back: That the mouse cell-type result needs checking in human cells: a mouse mechanism tied to a marker needs a human check of which cells carry it.
cards.quote: A mouse mechanism tied to a marker needs a human check of which cells carry it.
cards.section: Human atlases: methods, markers and denominators

cards.front: Two studies report likely human-specific DRG types, while the 2024 cross-species integration found none. Why does the integration not settle it?
cards.back: An integration is built to align data sets, so it can merge real differences between species.
cards.quote: an integration is built to align data sets and can merge real differences
cards.section: Design problem: is a proposed human-only class real?

cards.front: Validating a proposed human DRG class in tissue: why test two or three defining markers in the same neurons instead of one?
cards.back: A cluster is defined by a combination of expression, and one marker may be shared with other groups. Coexpression in the same cells tests whether the population exists, not just whether one gene is present.
cards.quote: A cluster is defined by a combination of expression, and one marker may be shared with other groups.
cards.section: Design problem: is a proposed human-only class real?

cards.front: A human-only DRG class gains a mouse partner only once mouse nuclei are compared with human nuclei at matched depth. What becomes the leading explanation, and what must be ruled out?
cards.back: A preparation difference, since whole-cell and nuclear data resolve different groups. One must still check that the integration did not force unlike groups together.
cards.why: Rests on the stated preparation warning: a mouse whole-cell Trpa1-rich group was missed in a nuclear data set.
cards.quote: a preparation difference becomes the leading explanation
cards.section: Design problem: is a proposed human-only class real?

cards.front: A proposed human DRG class survives matched preparations, several donors and clustering settings, and tissue validation, but recording finds no physiology distinct from its neighbours. How should it be described?
cards.back: As a molecular difference of unknown function: real as an expression difference, but with no functional type claim yet.
cards.why: The lesson's four-step test separates artefact, molecular difference and functional difference.
cards.quote: it is a molecular difference of unknown function
cards.section: Design problem: is a proposed human-only class real?

cards.front: All four validation steps support a human-mouse difference in a DRG class. What is still missing before calling the class human-specific?
cards.back: A comparison with another species, such as macaque. Two species can only show a human-mouse difference.
cards.quote: calling it human-specific also requires comparison with another species such as macaque
cards.section: Design problem: is a proposed human-only class real?

cards.front: In the robustness step of the lesson's test, which result marks a proposed class as fragile?
cards.back: A class carried by one donor, or by one clustering resolution or integration method. The class should recur across several donors and settings.
cards.why: Robustness is the stated second step, before tissue validation and functional anchoring.
cards.quote: A class carried by one donor or setting is fragile.
cards.section: Design problem: is a proposed human-only class real?

cards.front: Zeisel and colleagues profiled roughly half a million cells. Why is that number not a DRG-neuron sample size?
cards.back: It is the whole mouse nervous system census; only a part of it is peripheral sensory neurons.
cards.quote: That is the whole census, not a DRG-neuron count.
cards.section: Class lists, sample sizes and toolkit lines
